prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Whatever ’tis, whose beauty here below Attracts thee thus and makes thee stream and flow, And wind and curl, and wink and smile, Shifting thy gate and guile; Though thy close commerce nought at all imbars My present search, for eagles eye not stars, And still the lesser by the best And highest good is blest; Yet, seeing all things that subsist and be, Have their commissions from divinity, And teach us duty, I will see What man may learn from thee. First, I am sure, the subject so respected Is well dispos’d, for bodies once infected, Deprav’d, or dead, can have with thee No hold, nor sympathy. Next, there’s in it a restless, pure desire And longing for thy bright and vital fire, Desire that never will be quench’d, Nor can be writh’d, nor wrench’d. These are the magnets which so strongly move And work all night upon thy light and love, As beauteous shapes, we know not why, Command and guide the eye. For where desire, celestial, pure desire Hath taken root, and grows, and doth not tire, There God a commerce states, and sheds His secret on their heads. This is the heart he craves, and who so will But give it him, and grudge not, he shall feel That God is true, as herbs unseen Put on their youth and green.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Whatever, Attracts, And

outputs.L1:
Whatever ’tis whose beauty here below  
Attracts thee thus, and makes thee stream and flow,  
And wind and curl, and wink and smile,  
Shifting thy gait and guile;  

Though thy close commerce nought at all imbars  
My present search—for eagles eye not stars,  
And still the lesser by the best  
And highest good is blest—  

Yet, seeing all things that subsist and be  
Have their commissions from divinity,  
And teach us duty, I will see  
What man may learn from thee.  

First, I am sure the subject so respected  
Is well disposed; for bodies once infected,  
Depraved, or dead, can have with thee  
No hold, nor sympathy.  

Next, there’s in it a restless, pure desire,  
A longing for thy bright and vital fire—  
Desire that never will be quenched,  
Nor can be writhed, nor wrenched.  

These are the magnets which so strongly move  
And work all night upon thy light and love;  
As beauteous shapes, we know not why,  
Command and guide the eye.  

For where desire—celestial, pure desire—  
Hath taken root, and grows, and doth not tire,  
There God a commerce states, and sheds  
His secret on their heads.  

This is the heart He craves; and whoso will  
But give it Him, and grudge not, he shall feel  
That God is true, as herbs unseen  
Put on their youth and green.
outputs.L2:
Whatever it is here on earth whose loveliness draws you so powerfully, making you pour yourself out, move in winding curves, twist, flash, and seem to smile, changing your course and your subtle motions—still, your hidden dealings do not hinder my present inquiry. After all, eagles do not concern themselves with stars, and what is lower is blessed by what is best and highest.

Yet because everything that exists receives its charge from God and can instruct us in our duty, I will consider what human beings may learn from you.

First, I am certain that the thing you honor in this way must be rightly disposed; for bodies that are corrupted, diseased, or dead can have no connection or sympathy with you.

Next, within it there is a pure and tireless yearning, a longing for your bright, life-giving fire—a desire that cannot be extinguished, twisted aside, or forced away.

These are the powers that attract and move so strongly, working through the night upon your light and love, just as beautiful forms, for reasons we do not fully understand, direct and hold the gaze.

For wherever pure, heavenly desire has taken root, continues to grow, and does not grow weary, there God establishes communion and pours his hidden grace upon such souls.

This is the heart God seeks; and whoever willingly gives it to him without reluctance will discover that God is faithful—just as unseen plants put forth their freshness and green life.
outputs.L3:
The speaker begins by contemplating a beautiful and flowing force in nature, one that seems to move with grace, order, and quiet power. Rather than looking at it merely as a physical sight, the speaker seeks to understand it spiritually. The beauty of the natural world becomes a lesson, inviting the human soul to consider its own movement, purpose, and relationship with God.

In this vision, all created things receive their meaning and direction from divine wisdom. Nothing in creation exists without purpose; each creature, force, or natural process reflects something of the Creator’s will. Because of this, nature can become a teacher. By observing how created things follow the order given to them, human beings may learn their own duty: to turn toward God, to live according to divine purpose, and to seek the good for which they were made.

However, the speaker also recognizes that not everything can respond to beauty in the same way. The object drawn toward this beauty must be pure, receptive, and properly disposed. What is corrupted, lifeless, or inwardly disordered cannot truly participate in such beauty or be guided by it. In the same way, the soul must be cleansed of corruption and made open to grace if it is to be moved toward divine things.

The force that moves the soul is described as a restless yet pure desire for divine light. This desire does not allow the soul to remain satisfied with lower or passing things. Instead, it continually draws the soul upward, guiding it toward God as its true source and end. Such longing becomes the soul’s inner motion, a spiritual energy that directs it away from darkness and toward the brightness of divine truth.

When this pure desire takes root in the heart, God answers it with grace. The soul that sincerely longs for divine light is not abandoned; it is met by God’s secret and life-giving presence. Through this hidden grace, the heart is renewed, purified, and strengthened. The soul is transformed from within, learning to share more fully in the beauty it first observed in creation and to live in closer union with the divine purpose for which it was made.
outputs.L4:
The poem reflects on a natural phenomenon that moves continuously toward light, presenting it as more than a physical occurrence. Its flowing motion becomes a spiritual lesson, a sign placed in the world by God for human beings to contemplate. By observing its attraction to brightness and its refusal to remain still, the speaker suggests that nature reveals truths about the soul’s own desire for the divine.

The phenomenon is associated with purity, longing, and movement. It is drawn upward or onward not by force, but by an inward desire, just as the human heart is drawn toward what is holy. Its cleanness and brightness symbolize a soul freed from selfishness, while its constant motion represents spiritual striving. Through this image, the poem teaches that human beings should seek God with the same sincerity and steadiness.

In the end, the poem emphasizes that true longing is never wasted. When the heart remains pure and faithful in its desire, it attracts God’s hidden mercy and grace, even if that grace is not immediately visible. The closing image of unseen herbs turning green suggests quiet spiritual renewal: beneath the surface, life is being restored. In the same way, a willing and devoted heart is inwardly transformed by divine grace, becoming fresh, alive, and spiritually fertile.
outputs.L5:
**Whatever Attracts and Inspires**

Whatever attracts our attention often reveals something meaningful about who we are. It may be a dream, a goal, a person, or even a simple idea that sparks curiosity. Attraction is not always about appearance; it can come from kindness, confidence, creativity, and the energy something or someone brings into our lives.

When we notice what attracts us, we begin to understand our values and desires more clearly. Some people are attracted to adventure and change, while others are drawn to peace and stability. Whatever the source may be, it has the power to guide our choices and shape our journey.

In the end, whatever attracts us can also inspire us. It encourages growth, opens new paths, and helps us discover what truly matters.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a metaphysical devotional poem in the style of Henry Vaughan, using archaic diction, rhymed couplets, and a meditation on a natural phenomenon that teaches the soul about divine desire.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Magnet-Stone**

I saw a stone, deep hid in earth’s cold womb,  
Draw secret iron through the silent gloom;  

No hand it had, yet held; no voice, yet cried,  
And made the dull, dark metal leave its side.  

“Poor soul,” quoth I, “what loadstone thus in thee  
Can stir thy dust, and make thy bondage flee?”  

Then from the hill there brake a beam of light,  
And all my inward caverns leapt from night.  

I knew Thee then, sweet Lord, whose hidden art  
Doth woo the iron winter of my heart;  

Thy love, unseen, runs through this clod of clay,  
And draws my buried heaviness away.  

O blessed Force! O mild Almighty Chain!  
That bind’st by freedom, and dost loose by pain;  

Still pull me upward, till my dross be gone,  
And I, all Thine, move only to Thy throne.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a pastiche of an English metaphysical poet like George Herbert or Henry Vaughan, with themes of attraction, purity, celestial desire, and the soul’s communion with divinity.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Magnet of the Soul**

Lord, Thou art North; and I, a trembling steel,  
Long lain in dust, and ignorant of pole,  
Feel through my rust Thy secret virtue steal,  
And draw the vagrant filings of my soul.

What loadstone lodgeth in Thy wounded side,  
That all my scattered loves run there and cling?  
The stars, like silver bees, forsake their hive  
To taste the brightness of so pure a Spring.

O make me clean, not with the snow’s cold art,  
Which hides the mire, yet leaves the earth unblest;  
But with that fire which, entering at the heart,  
Burns dross to prayer, and turns the smoke to rest.

For I have courted lamps, and called them suns,  
Kissed painted angels on a window’s glass;  
But when Thy morning through my darkness runs,  
All lesser beauties blush away, and pass.

Then let my will, that little wandering sphere,  
Move in Thy music, and no longer range;  
Each appetite become a crystal clear,  
Each earthly motion suffer heavenly change.

So shall I rise, yet rise by being drawn,  
As dew ascends, obedient to the day;  
And in Thy light, more chaste than star or dawn,  
Lose not myself—but find myself in Thee.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an archaic Christian lyric poem about observing something in nature that streams, curls, and shines, then drawing moral and spiritual lessons from it.
counterfactuals.output:
**Upon a Sunlit Brook**

I marked, at prime, a little brook  
Come stealing from the hill;  
It sang where bending alders shook,  
And brake the meadow still.  

It streamed in silver, soft and fleet,  
It curled round stone and thorn;  
And on its face, with trembling feet,  
The gold of heaven was borne.  

“Ah me,” quoth I, “so run my days,  
Through briar, shade, and gleam;  
Now dark with earth, now bright with rays,  
Yet hastening like this stream.  

Teach me, sweet brook, thy lowly art,  
To pass and murmur praise;  
To keep a clear and pilgrim heart  
Through all my winding ways.  

For though thou bend, thou dost not bide;  
Though rocks thy course constrain,  
Still onward to the ampler tide  
Thou journeyest amain.  

So let my soul, by grief made meek,  
By grace made pure and free,  
Through this dim vale her Ocean seek,  
O Christ, and rest in Thee.  

And as thy wave, with heavenly fire,  
Doth catch the morning’s flame,  
Lord, kindle all my dull desire  
To shine unto Thy Name.  

Then, when these mortal banks are past,  
And time’s poor reeds are riven,  
Receive me in Thy deep at last—  
The boundless Sea of Heaven.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a rhyming devotional poem in early modern English that argues all created things have “commissions from divinity” and can instruct mankind in faith.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Creatures’ Charge**

Mark, man, the world: each herb and tree  
Hath **commissions from divinity**;  
The lark that climbeth toward the sun  
Preacheth, “Thy praise be first begun.”

The brook, that murmureth through the stone,  
Saith, “Hearts made hard are not thine own;  
Let grace run soft, let mercy be  
A stream to bear thee to the sea.”

The lily, clad withouten care,  
Doth chide thy pride, rebuke thy fear:  
“If God so deck a fading flower,  
Trust thou His hand in darker hour.”

The ant, beneath her burden bent,  
Cries, “Sluggard, learn thy day is lent;  
Lay up good works, whilst light is given,  
And make thy little cell for heaven.”

The thunder, with his awful breath,  
Proclaims the Judge, the grave, and death;  
Yet after wrath the rainbow saith,  
“His covenant outliveth faith.”

The stars, those candles of the night,  
Do spell His name in silver light;  
They teach the soul, when earth is dim,  
To steer her pilgrimage by Him.

Yea, dust and worm, and thorn and clod,  
Are schoolmen in the house of God;  
No creature dumb, but hath a tongue  
To tell whereof its Lord hath sung.

Then bend thine ear, thou child of clay;  
The fields are chapels by the way.  
Who readeth well this book abroad  
Shall find each leaf a line of God.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
